newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - FOMC, US jobs, UK budget to feature.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - FOMC, US jobs, UK budget to feature.

text.p: Financial markets face a turbulent week as they navigate their way through a U.S. Federal Reserve policy meeting, and key June payrolls data, analysts said.
The action-packed week also includes a British budget on Wednesday, expected to include fiscal tightening to take some heat off the simmering UK economy.

"There is the potential for the UK to underperform against Bunds this week but generally European bonds will likely outperform the U.S.," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi Int'l here.
"Assuming market expectations are correct and the Fed doesn't move rates at the FOMC, the focus will be more on payrolls," he said.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting is on Tuesday and Wednesday while U.S. labour market data will be released on Thursday because of the Independence Day holiday on Friday.

Chester said he was looking for quite a sharp bounce in the June non-farm payrolls data, which rose 138,000 in May. He said he expected a 250,000 rise in June as seasonal factors unwind and fundamentals point to job gains.
"We may get a slight bid higher if the FOMC do announce a no change in rates, but any relief bid will be temporary. I can't see many people going long into Thursday," said Chester.

Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe, said assuming no rate change on Wednesday, strong payrolls data may spark speculation the Fed is behind the curve, opening the risk of Treasuries' underperforming Europe.
"No one is looking for a rate rise, so the upside would be limited. The way Treasuries have been trading recently suggests the market is a bit vulnerable," he said.

Ian Harwood, head of strategy and economics at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities in London, noted a strong figure from the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) figure on Tuesday may upset U.S. interest rate expectations.

"Everybody's agreed that rates will stay on hold, but the only thing that could upset that is if the NAPM were to be very strong, particularly if the inflation indicators were to deteriorate," he said.
Chester said in Britain, Wednesday's budget would captivate gilts in the earlier part of the week.
"The big question in the UK is the balance of policy mix (between monetary and fiscal)," he said.

"If (the Chancellor) does tighten fiscal policy it will be supportive, but if he doesn't the inevitable concern is that monetary policy will have to rise more sharply than would otherwise be the case so there would be disappointment in the short end," said Chester.
The Confederation of British Industry distributive trades survey on Thursday will also be watched for the first signs of how strong retail activity was in June.
In the rest of Europe, German industrial production data for May was scheduled for release sometime between Thursday and Monday.
"I don't think the data will upset expectations much," said Harwood. "They will suggest the German recovery remains on its feet but very much export led."
French unemployment data was due on Monday.
